`{winpipe}` exposes Win32 Named Pipes as R connections to read from and write to. Named Pipes are a device for inter-process communication (IPC) that are part of the file system and allow for fine-grained access control. R has native support for FIFOs on Unix-like systems but does not expose any API for named pipes on Windows.

Features:

* Create and serve Windows named pipes, i.e., R can be both client and server
* Named pipes are represented as native R connections, i.e., I/O works out of the box
* Let R talk to non-R processes
* Can accept clients without blocking the R session
* Includes an interface to [SDDL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/security-descriptor-definition-language) 

## Installation

You can install the development version of winpipe from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("jslth/winpipe")
```

## Example

To communicate between processes, a server and a client are required:

```{r connection}
library(winpipe)

server <- winpipe("a-pipe")
client <- winpipe("a-pipe", server = FALSE)
```

Since winpipes are R connections, most I/O functions work out of the box. You can, for example, pass the client as a file name to `write.csv()`:

```{r write}
write.csv(iris, file = client)
```

The server can then receive the data. Depending on the permissions, this works in both directions (client → server and server → client)

```{r read}
head(read.csv(server))
```

Beware, however, that reading consumes a payload. Another call to `read.csv()` would result in an error. You can peek a payload without consuming it using `np_peek()`. This confirms that the payload has been consumed by giving the number of bytes left to read.

```{r peek}
np_peek(server)
```

One cool thing about named pipes is their access control. Named pipes support security descriptors using [DACL](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discretionary_Access_Control) and `{winpipe}` includes a small API to construct ACLs. To allow only admins and the local system to access a named pipe, you can do:

```{r dacl}
sd <- sd_create(
  ace(type = "deny", rights = "generic all", account = "everyone"),
  ace(type = "allow", rights = "generic all", account = "admins"),
  ace(type = "allow", rights = "generic all", account = "local system")
)
sd
```

A winpipe created with this security descriptor will deny access to all non-privileged users. You can pass this security descriptor to a pipe you create and it will adhere to this access control. `np_sd()` allows you to read the security descriptor of a given named pipe (note that Windows "normalizes" the descriptor, so it might not look like your input).

```{r dacl-test}
pipe <- winpipe("sd-pipe", sddl = sd)
np_sd(pipe)
```

```{r dacl-close, echo=FALSE}
close(server)
close(client)
close(pipe)
```


## Related work

* [`processx`](https://processx.r-lib.org/) can emulate named pipes as child processes
* [`httppipe`](https://github.com/richfitz/httppipe) uses `reticulate` to communicate with named pipes through Python
